issues.item: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, a trigger based on being in a similar natural environment is hard to reconcile unless the robbery specifically occurred in wilderness or outdoors; nothing else in the profile supports that context, making this trigger clinically incongruent with the rest of the presentation.

Helicopter/aircraft sounds are not a plausible trauma-linked trigger for a mugging/robbery in the absence of any supporting memory or threat content suggesting emergency-response, combat, or disaster context. This appears disconnected from the trauma type and the rest of the selected items.

For a mugging/robbery trauma, helicopter/aircraft sounds are hard to link clinically unless the robbery specifically involved aircraft or a major police response; this trigger is not supported by the other selected items and feels trauma-incongruent.

Alcohol smell could occur if the perpetrator had been drinking, but that link is not reflected anywhere else in the profile, so as selected it appears weakly grounded in the trauma narrative compared with the other more plausible interpersonal-danger cues.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma in a 67-year-old male, contamination and body-focused shame are hard to reconcile unless there was a sexual assault or severe bodily violation component, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile. These appraisals fit poorly with the stated trauma type and with the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Burnt smell is a highly specific trigger that suggests fire, smoke, or explosion exposure. In a robbery/mugging profile it lacks support from the threat and appraisal items and does not connect plausibly to the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery in a 67-year-old male, 'body shame' is hard to reconcile unless there was prominent sexual assault, disfigurement, or injury-focused trauma content, which is not reflected elsewhere in threat, memory, or strategies. It reads as a qualitatively different appraisal from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: 'Burnt smell' is not a plausible trigger for a mugging/robbery unless there was specific fire/smoke/burning content in the trauma, which is not supported by the other selected items. It appears disconnected from the stated trauma type and from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery victim, 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the least coherent item in the profile. The rest of the report centers on external danger and mistrust (suspicious people, loud noises, hypervigilance, alarm when touched, mistrust, humiliation), but this item implies morally dissonant behaviour by the patient during the event. That is possible, but without any supporting memory or strategy content it stands apart from the otherwise victimization-focused formulation and is harder to reconcile clinically than the other items. The remaining items are broadly coherent with robbery trauma and with the active formulation path Negative Appraisals → Threat and Threat → Triggers.

vignette: Six months ago, Arthur Vance was walking back to the staff entrance of the Grandview Hotel after reviewing a late audit. The autumn air was crisp until he passed a parked sedan where a man stood swaying, a sharp, sour odor of fermented alcohol clinging to his jacket. Arthur felt a prickle at the base of his neck, but he kept walking, his eyes fixed on the glass doors ahead. Then the man stepped forward, his hand reaching out. Arthur tried to sidestep, but the man's grip locked onto his coat lapel. When Arthur pulled back, his keys dropped to the pavement, clattering loudly against the concrete. The sound seemed to shatter the street. The man shoved him hard against the brick wall, the impact knocking the air from his lungs, and demanded his wallet. Arthur froze, his mind going blank as the man snatched it and vanished into the alley. The violation of having his property and his dignity stripped away in seconds left him shaking on the sidewalk, certain that the city had turned predatory in the span of a heartbeat. In the weeks that followed, Arthur's daily rhythm shifted. He had come to believe that the streets were fundamentally dangerous, a place where a single wrong turn could put him at the mercy of strangers. At the hotel, this sense of threat sat alongside his waking hours. When guests approached the front desk with hurried steps or lingered too long in the lobby shadows, Arthur found himself tracking their hands and eye lines, his shoulders permanently tense. He stopped attending the evening staff dinners. The sight of the hotel bar's opening hours made his stomach turn; the faint whiff of whiskey from a guest's coat sent a sudden, cold warning through his chest. He would quickly turn his collar up and take a longer route to the administrative offices, telling himself he simply preferred the quiet. Loud sounds, once the background hum of a busy hotel, now struck him like physical blows. A dropped tray in the breakfast kitchen or a keycard reader beeping too loudly made his jaw clench and his breath shorten. He couldn't explain why the noise mattered so much, but it felt like a precursor to something he had no defense against. At home, the quiet of his marriage became a source of vigilance rather than comfort. Arthur slept with the bedroom door closed and the hallway light left on. He checked the deadbolt three times every night, listening for footsteps on the walkway that weren't there. When his wife, Clara, reached out to guide his arm as they walked past the kitchen counter, his body reacted before his mind could catch up. He jerked away with a sharp gasp, his pulse hammering against his ribs. He apologized immediately, telling her he had just been startled, but he was certain that his own reflexes were the only thing keeping him safe. The humiliation of the mugging lingered in his chest like a bruise. He felt permanently marked by it, a man who had been cornered and helpless. He avoided talking about the incident, convinced that mentioning it would only underscore how exposed he still felt. Alongside these experiences, his management style shifted. He began questioning the intentions of his evening shift supervisors, insisting on seeing every guest report signed in triplicate. He stopped taking the short cut through the service corridor, opting instead to walk the full perimeter of the lobby, counting cameras and monitoring sightlines. His staff noticed the change. His wife noticed the distance. They had asked him to visit a clinic, but Arthur had hesitated. What frightened him most was that the trigger was still waiting outside, that the world had not changed even if he had. It was the morning he had flinched away from a colleague's handshake so violently that he had knocked a stack of room key cards to the floor that finally pushed him to the consultation door. Sitting in the waiting area, listening to the muffled sounds of the hotel district, he felt a profound exhaustion. He did not want to live like a guest in his own life anymore. He was hoping, more than anything, to learn how to trust the ground beneath his feet again, and to stop feeling the sting of that sidewalk every time a door opened.
